bibliographic.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Generative AI, and Agentic AI Governance: An Integrated Enterprise Governance Prioritization Architecture
bibliographic.citation_apa: Rah, A., & Hahues, S. (2026). Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Generative AI, and Agentic AI Governance: An Integrated Enterprise Governance Prioritization Architecture. Research Square. https://doi.org/10.21203/rs.3.rs-10012178/v1

methodology.method_family: Design Science Research with exploratory platform-risk analysis, rubric-based dataset scoring, Monte Carlo robustness assessment, framework coverage matrix, and public-document relevance assessment
methodology.study_design: Proposed integrated governance architecture (EAPT, EART, EAGM, IAGF) connected via Governance Priority Score (GPS), evaluated on a rubric-based dataset of 19 enterprise AI platforms across eight risk subdimensions
methodology.sample_description: 19 enterprise AI platforms scored across eight subdimensions (data access scope, operational autonomy, tool/API integration breadth, external connectivity, governance burden, cybersecurity exposure, adoption and shadow-AI risk, supply-chain integrity); public evidence from U.S. government agencies, universities, healthcare systems, and financial institutions used for relevance assessment
methodology.sector: Enterprise AI across multiple sectors including government, healthcare, and financial institutions
methodology.technology_context: Generative AI (GenAI), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), agentic AI, large language models embedded in productivity suites, cloud platforms, customer-service workflows, and domain-specific enterprise applications

eligibility.decision_rationale: The article directly develops an integrated enterprise governance prioritization architecture for GenAI, RAG, and agentic AI, linking platform burden, governance-risk exposure, organizational readiness, agentic runtime-control needs, and executive decision support through GPS. It explicitly addresses audit, cybersecurity, executive oversight, standards (NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, EU AI Act, OWASP LLM Top 10), and regulated-sector public evidence, aligning closely with the review scope on governance of LLM-based systems in high-stakes environments.
eligibility.manual_spotcheck_reason: Only partial front matter, abstract, introduction, methods excerpts, and keyword hits were supplied; full-text verification is needed to confirm conversational-AI specificity, human oversight mechanisms, observability/audit operational detail, and complete limitations.

appraisal.notes: Design-science fit is strong for architecture contribution. Authors explicitly state Monte Carlo/Spearman results reflect internal coding stability and robustness, not external validation. Three-stage literature/source selection is described but full screening protocol detail is incomplete in provided excerpts.

cerqual.explanation: Framework components (EAPT, EART, EAGM, IAGF, GPS) are coherently integrated and highly relevant to enterprise governance of RAG, GenAI, and agentic AI. Confidence is moderated because evaluation relies on author-coded platform-risk rubrics and public-document relevance assessment without reported external validation, inter-rater reliability, or organizational pilot evidence in the supplied text.

synthesis.main_claim: Enterprise adoption of GenAI, RAG, and agentic AI outpaces governance adaptation; the authors propose an integrated governance prioritization architecture that operationally connects platform burden, governance-risk gaps, organizational readiness, and agentic runtime-control needs through GPS.
synthesis.contribution: Introduces and integrates EAPT, EART, EAGM, and IAGF within a unified workflow supported by a reproducible 19-platform rubric dataset, Monte Carlo robustness testing, framework coverage matrix, and GPS-based demonstration, drawing on major AI governance and security standards.
synthesis.limitations: Authors characterize the work as a bounded design-science foundation for future validation; scoring robustness is presented as internal coding stability (Spearman's rho = 0.996) rather than external validation; conversational-system governance is referenced indirectly via customer-service workflows and agentic controls rather than as a primary focus.
synthesis.use_in_review: Use as central evidence for enterprise-level governance architectures spanning RAG, GenAI, and agentic AI; for GPS-style prioritization of controls; and for mapping to NIST, ISO/IEC 42001, EU AI Act, OWASP LLM Top 10, and MITRE ATLAS in regulated enterprise contexts.
